title: Cannula (Needle) Cricothyroidotomy & Rescue Oxygenation
keywords: it oxygenates at best — it does not ventilate, protect the airway, or take PEEP
failed in roughly 60% of NAP4 cannula attempts; 18% vs 83% rescue oxygenation success against scalpel-bougie in a porcine model
expiration is the problem, not inspiration — an obstructed upper airway plus jet insufflation is how barotrauma happens
a bridge with a clock on it: CO2 climbs and it needs converting
sources: Cook TM, Woodall N, Frerk C. Major complications of airway management in the UK: 4th National Audit Project (NAP4). Br J Anaesth. 2011;106(5):617-631 (cannula cricothyroidotomy failed in roughly 60% of cases).

Heard AMB, et al. Rescue oxygenation success by cannula or scalpel-bougie emergency front-of-neck access in an anaesthetised porcine model. Br J Anaesth. 2020;124(3):293-300 (rescue oxygenation succeeded in 18% after cannula vs 83% after scalpel-bougie; device placement 73% vs 92%).
Ahmad I, El-Boghdadly K, Bhagrath R, et al. Difficult Airway Society 2025 guidelines for management of unanticipated difficult tracheal intubation in adults. Br J Anaesth. 2026;136(2):283-307.
Whatling J, et al. Adult front of neck airway: a narrative review. J Oral Maxillofac Anesth. 2024 (narrow-bore limitations, Ventrain, hypercarbia limiting use to roughly 30-40 minutes).
Haag B, et al. Emergency front-of-neck access in pediatric anesthesia: a narrative review. Paediatr Anaesth. 2024;34(10).

changelog.change: New — one of the four technique subsections in the CICO & Front-of-Neck Access category. No cannula technique existed anywhere in the guide; CICO content went straight to the scalpel, which left the pediatric bridge and the no-kit scenario unaddressed.

purpose: The cannula technique and the rescue-oxygenation devices that follow it — how to do it, when it is still the right call, and an honest account of why it is no longer the adult default.
entryPrompt: Read the failure data before you plan to rely on this. It remains worth knowing: it is sometimes the only kit in the room, and in small children it is sometimes the only anatomy you have.

nodes.prompt: Read this before you choose it
nodes.body: The evidence against cannula cricothyroidotomy as an adult default is not marginal.

items: NAP4: cannula cricothyroidotomy failed in roughly 60% of the cases audited, while surgical technique was near-uniformly successful.
In an anesthetized porcine CICO model, rescue oxygenation succeeded in 18% after cannula versus 83% after scalpel-bougie; even device placement was 73% versus 92%.
The failure is rarely the puncture. It is kinking, displacement into the pretracheal tissues, and an inability to confirm you are where you think you are before you insufflate.

items.text: It is not an airway. It is an oxygen line.
items: No protection from gastric contents.
No PEEP.
CO2 accumulates — a narrow-bore cannula is generally a 30-40 minute proposition before respiratory acidosis becomes the problem you are treating.

nodes.prompt: 1 · When it is still the right call
nodes.body: Three situations, and none of them is 'because it feels less drastic'.

items: It is genuinely the only kit in the room and nobody can improvise a scalpel technique.
The operator has no surgical airway training at all and a cannula is what they have actually practised.
A small child, where the cricothyroid membrane will not take a tube — as a bridge while a surgical tracheotomy is being set up. See the pediatric card.
As a deliberate first move that does not preclude escalation: a cannula in the neck does not stop you cutting, and the skin mark it leaves tells the next operator where the midline is.

nodes.body: Extend the neck if the cervical spine allows. Stabilize the larynx with the non-dominant hand and identify the cricothyroid membrane with the laryngeal handshake.

items: Attach a cannula-over-needle (a purpose-made kink-resistant airway cannula if you have one; a 14G IV cannula is the improvised fallback and kinks readily) to a syringe containing a few milliliters of saline or air.
Puncture in the midline through the cricothyroid membrane, angled 45 degrees CAUDALLY, aspirating continuously.

items.text: Free aspiration of air is your confirmation. Stop advancing the needle the moment you get it.
items: Bubbles through saline are easier to read than an air-filled syringe in a bloody field.
No aspiration means you are not in the airway. Do not insufflate on hope — insufflating into tissue destroys the anatomy for everyone who follows.
Advance the cannula off the needle, hold it at the skin, and withdraw the needle.
RE-ASPIRATE through the cannula alone to confirm it is still intraluminal. This step is skipped constantly and is where the technique is lost.
Hold the cannula manually for its entire life. It is not secure, it will kink, and letting go of it is how it ends up in the pretracheal tissue.

nodes.prompt: 3 · Rescue oxygenation — and the exhalation problem
nodes.body:
This is where cannula technique is genuinely dangerous, and the danger is not getting oxygen in. It is getting it out.

A narrow cannula plus a completely obstructed upper airway means gas enters under pressure and has nowhere to leave. Stacked breaths become barotrauma, pneumothorax, and cardiovascular collapse — sometimes within a few insufflations.

items.text: Whatever device you use, the rule is the same: insufflate briefly, then WATCH AND WAIT for the chest to fall before the next breath.
items: Inspiratory times of about 1 second with expiratory pauses several times longer.
If the chest is not falling, stop. Open the upper airway — reposition, jaw thrust, adjuncts, or a supraglottic airway left in place as an exhalation route.

A high-pressure jet source (Manujet or similar) delivers volume through a narrow lumen but is exactly the device that causes barotrauma when exhalation is obstructed. It requires a deliberate operator, not a hopeful one.

The Ventrain and similar flow-controlled devices assist EXPIRATION as well as inspiration and can achieve close to a normal minute volume through a 2 mm internal-diameter catheter. If your department stocks one, it is the device this technique was waiting for.

Low-pressure sources — a bag-valve via a 3.0 tube connector, or wall oxygen with a Y-piece — will oxygenate poorly and ventilate essentially not at all. They are better than nothing and should not be mistaken for more than that.
Monitor for surgical emphysema continuously. A neck that is visibly swelling means gas is going somewhere other than the trachea, and the cannula has failed.

nodes.prompt: 4 · Convert it, and start the clock when you site it
nodes.body: A cannula is a bridge with a time limit. Plan the definitive airway from the moment it starts working, not from the moment it stops.

items: Escalate to a definitive airway — scalpel-bougie, a formal tracheostomy, or a controlled oral intubation once oxygenation has bought conditions for one.
If oxygenation is not restored promptly, do not keep adjusting the cannula. Move to a scalpel technique. Repeated cannula attempts are the documented failure pattern.
Imaging for pneumothorax and surgical emphysema once stable, and a low threshold for a chest drain if positive-pressure ventilation is continuing.
Document the time sited, the time converted, and whether aspiration was confirmed before insufflation.

checklist: Chose cannula for a stated reason — kit, training, or pediatric anatomy — not by default
Free aspiration confirmed BEFORE the needle was advanced and again through the cannula alone
Cannula held manually at all times
Insufflation brief, with the chest watched for fall before the next breath
Upper airway kept as open as possible as an exhalation route
Definitive airway planned from the moment the cannula started working
buildNote: New in the CICO batch. Written as an honest appraisal rather than a neutral how-to: NAP4's roughly 60% failure and the 18% vs 83% porcine rescue-oxygenation figures are stated up front, in a warning node, because the technique's main danger is being chosen for the wrong reason. The exhalation/barotrauma physiology gets its own step — it is the part that kills and the part most commonly taught as an afterthought. Ventrain is named because flow-controlled expiration is the one thing that changes the risk calculus.
